paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from a limited collection of data, making regularization important for avoiding overfitting. One-step methods make a single policy improvement, offering a simple and stable approach whose eventual performance can be limited. Critic-regularization methods instead make repeated improvements using a regularized objective, typically spending more computation while offering appealing lower-bound guarantees.

The paper connects these seemingly different strategies. Under its theoretical assumptions, setting the regularization coefficient of a multi-step critic-regularization method to one produces the same policy as one-step reinforcement learning. This means that repeated optimization and a single improvement can arrive at the same result under a particular regularization choice.

The equivalence depends on assumptions that include deterministic dynamics, so it is a conditional theoretical result. Experiments with CQL and one-step methods nevertheless show that the analysis makes accurate, testable predictions using commonly chosen hyperparameters. The contribution is both a conceptual link between algorithm families and evidence that this link helps explain practical offline learning behavior.
icml-2023-a-connection-between-one-step-.tldr: Under stated assumptions, a particular critic-regularization setting makes multi-step offline reinforcement learning produce the same policy as one-step learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find the k closest reference points for every point in a query collection. The reference set contains n points and the query set contains m points, with distances defined by a metric. The goal is to organize the reference points so that answering many queries has a near-linear running time.

Earlier cover-tree analyses claimed efficient construction and search, but subsequent work identified a serious gap in a search-time argument and counterexamples to a key step used in both proofs. This paper addresses those obstacles with a simpler structure called a compressed cover tree and supplies new construction and search algorithms.

The stated construction time is O(n log n), while processing all queries takes O(m(k + log n) log k). These bounds hide a dimensionality factor that depends on how the reference and query points are distributed, rather than on the sizes of the sets. That qualification matters when interpreting near-linear scaling: the contribution establishes improved algorithmic foundations while retaining a dependence on the geometry of the data.
icml-2023-a-new-near-linear-time-algorit.tldr: A compressed cover tree supports new near-linear construction and nearest-neighbor search bounds, with a hidden factor depending on point distributions.

paragraphs: Generative diffusion models commonly learn to reverse a process that adds Gaussian noise. Many kinds of data instead occupy discrete states, motivating a formulation built directly around discrete changes. This paper develops a theoretical framework that allows arbitrary discrete-state Markov processes to serve as the forward diffusion process.

The analysis is exact rather than variational. It identifies the reverse-time stochastic process and corresponding score function for continuous time, and the reverse-time mapping for discrete time. By relating these results to Gaussian diffusion and existing discrete approaches, the framework clarifies how different diffusion constructions fit together.

Blackout Diffusion provides a concrete example: it learns to generate an image starting from an empty image rather than a noisy one. Experiments on CIFAR-10, Binarized MNIST, and CelebA establish that this approach is feasible. The stated finding supports a broader choice of forward processes and starting states for generation; its significance lies in demonstrating this flexibility and providing an exact theoretical account of it.
icml-2023-blackout-diffusion-generative-.tldr: Blackout Diffusion demonstrates image generation from an empty image within an exact framework for discrete-state diffusion processes.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a model on tasks encountered over time, raising the question of how later learning affects earlier tasks. This paper examines that question for linear classification with binary labels and separable task data. This setting gives the authors a precise mathematical basis for studying forgetting.

The main connection is that learning with weak regularization reduces to a sequence of maximum-margin problems. These problems favor separating boundaries with large margins and correspond to a particular case of Projection Onto Convex Sets. The connection translates the learning sequence into a geometric framework that can be analyzed mathematically.

Using this framework, the authors derive upper bounds on forgetting and other quantities when tasks recur, including in cyclic and random orders. They discuss implications for how regularization is scheduled and weighted during training. They also identify theoretical differences from continual regression, showing why conclusions about one learning setting need care when transferred to another. The results concern the stated separable linear-classification setting and its weak-regularization analysis.
icml-2023-continual-learning-in-linear-c.tldr: For separable linear classification, weakly regularized continual learning connects to sequential maximum-margin problems, enabling theoretical bounds on forgetting.

paragraphs: In a delayed bandit problem, a learner chooses among K actions but learns the resulting loss only later. This paper adds an immediate observation: a state from a finite collection. It asks whether that early signal can improve decisions while the final feedback remains delayed.

The answer depends on how states relate to losses, regardless of whether actions lead to states stochastically or adversarially. With adversarial state-to-loss relationships and fixed delay d, regret scales as the square root of (K + d)T, up to logarithmic factors. This matches the rate without intermediate observations, so those observations do not improve the regret rate in this regime.

When state-to-loss relationships are stochastic, the rate instead involves the smaller of the number of states and the delay. Intermediate observations therefore help when there are fewer states than delay steps. The paper also gives refined high-probability upper bounds for varying delays and experimentally validates its algorithms. The distinction identifies when immediate information has enough statistical structure to reduce the cost of waiting.
icml-2023-delayed-bandits-when-do-interm.tldr: Intermediate observations improve delayed-bandit regret rates when state-to-loss relationships are stochastic and the state count is smaller than the delay.

paragraphs: Some machine learning selection problems require minimizing the difference between two submodular functions. A known mathematical connection rewrites this as minimizing the difference between two convex functions. The paper argues that existing algorithms have not fully used this connection and develops methods that make it central to optimization.

The authors adapt the classical difference-of-convex algorithm, DCA, and its complete form, CDCA, to the corresponding continuous formulation. They extend convergence results for DCA and connect those results back to the original submodular problem. This step matters because guarantees about the reformulated problem need to explain what happens in the selection problem itself.

For DCA, the resulting guarantees match those of existing submodular-difference algorithms while describing convergence more fully. CDCA provides a stronger guarantee of local minimality, which concerns the quality of a solution relative to nearby alternatives. Numerical experiments on speech corpus selection and feature selection show the proposed algorithms outperforming existing baselines. Together, the theory and experiments support exploiting the convex connection more directly.
icml-2023-difference-of-submodular-minim.tldr: Adapting difference-of-convex optimization improves convergence understanding and yields stronger local guarantees for minimizing differences of submodular functions.

paragraphs: Geometric graph learning can use both the arrangement of points and the structure of their connections. This paper combines these sources of information in Equivariant Message Passing Simplicial Networks, or EMPSNs. The models respond consistently when inputs are rotated, translated, or reflected.

EMPSNs learn features for higher-dimensional simplices, such as triangles, allowing them to use geometric information associated with groups of connected points. They extend equivariant graph neural networks to richer topological structures while also adding geometry to message-passing simplicial networks. This makes the architecture a proof of concept for combining geometric and topological learning within one model.

The reported results indicate generally better performance than either component approach alone and performance comparable to leading methods for geometric graphs. They also suggest that including geometry helps counter over-smoothing, where repeated message passing makes representations too similar. This effect appears especially useful with higher-dimensional simplicial structures. The findings support the value of combining the two kinds of information, while the over-smoothing conclusion remains an experimental suggestion.
icml-2023-e-n-equivariant-message-passin.tldr: EMPSNs combine symmetry-respecting geometry with higher-dimensional graph structure, improving reported performance and showing evidence of reduced over-smoothing.

paragraphs: Materials models often need predictions that respect spatial symmetries: changing a structure's orientation or position should leave some outputs unchanged and transform others consistently. Graph neural networks can enforce these requirements through their architecture, but such restrictions can reduce expressivity, scalability, or how readily the model can be understood.

The paper introduces a model-independent framework based on stochastic frame averaging. It enforces E(3) invariance or equivariance without placing symmetry constraints on the underlying architecture. This separates the mechanism that respects spatial symmetry from the design of the network that processes geometric information.

FAENet is the accompanying graph neural network, designed to be simple, fast, and expressive while using this framework. The authors prove the method's validity and report superior accuracy and computational scalability on materials tasks from OC20 and molecular tasks from QM9 and QM7-X. The contribution is therefore both a general way to impose symmetry and a concrete model showing its usefulness across the stated modeling tasks.
icml-2023-faenet-frame-averaging-equivar.tldr: FAENet uses stochastic frame averaging to respect spatial symmetries without architectural constraints, with reported gains in materials and molecular modeling.

paragraphs: Selecting a representative subset from a large dataset involves balancing usefulness against the cost of processing the data. Streaming submodular maximization provides a model for this task. When the data includes sensitive attributes such as race or gender, selection also needs to account for fairness to help avoid biased outcomes.

Previous fair-selection work considered a cardinality constraint, which limits how many items can be chosen. This paper moves to matroid constraints, a more general way of specifying allowable selections. The change expands the selection problem beyond controlling the subset's size while retaining a formal structure for algorithm design.

The authors provide streaming algorithms together with impossibility results that characterize trade-offs among efficiency, solution quality, and fairness. Including both achievable results and barriers clarifies what compromises the problem can require. Experiments examine exemplar-based clustering, movie recommendation, and maximum coverage in social networks. These applications provide empirical validation of the findings across several representative-subset tasks, connecting the theoretical trade-offs to concrete selection settings.
icml-2023-fairness-in-streaming-submodul.tldr: The paper develops fair streaming selection algorithms under matroid constraints and characterizes trade-offs between efficiency, quality, and fairness.

paragraphs: Gaussian process state-space models describe how an unobserved state evolves and produces observations at discrete times. Their flexibility comes with a difficult inference problem: many hidden variables must be estimated, and those variables are strongly connected through time. Simplifying these relationships too aggressively can lose useful structure, while richer inference can require substantial computation.

The paper proposes free-form variational inference using stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo within an inducing-variable formulation. The approach addresses the simplifying assumptions and computational demands of previous methods. Its proposed variational distribution also permits a collapsed extension, in which inducing variables are integrated out analytically rather than retained as variables to estimate.

The authors additionally demonstrate combinations with particle MCMC methods. Across six real-world datasets, their approach learns transition dynamics and latent states more accurately than competing methods. These results concern both parts of the modeling task: recovering the hidden trajectory and learning how it changes over time. The work provides an inference framework intended to preserve useful temporal structure while making Bayesian GPSSMs more practical.
icml-2023-free-form-variational-inferenc.tldr: A free-form variational inference framework improves latent-state and transition-dynamics estimation for Gaussian process state-space models on six real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can be strengthened by adding information that helps distinguish nodes and describe their structural positions. Two common approaches use random features or spectral positional encodings. This paper connects them through Random Feature Propagation, or RFP, rather than treating them as separate design choices.

RFP begins with random node features and repeatedly propagates them using a graph-dependent operator. Its construction draws on iterative methods for computing dominant eigenvectors. Crucially, it concatenates several intermediate steps, retaining information from the progression of the iteration. The propagation operator can be chosen beforehand or learned.

The authors provide theoretical reasons for using random features, keeping early propagation steps, and combining multiple random initializations. They then show that RFP significantly outperforms both random features and spectral positional encodings on multiple node- and graph-classification benchmarks. The results indicate that the route from random initialization toward spectral structure contains useful information of its own, giving a principled reason to preserve intermediate representations in a positional encoding.
icml-2023-graph-positional-encoding-via-.tldr: Random Feature Propagation builds graph positional encodings from intermediate propagation steps, outperforming random-feature and spectral alternatives on multiple benchmarks.

paragraphs: Comparing reinforcement learning algorithms fairly requires attention to how their settings are chosen. The paper shows that hyperparameters can substantially affect both final performance and sample efficiency. It also finds that which settings look good can depend strongly on the random seed used during tuning, creating a risk of overfitting to that seed.

The authors recommend established automated machine learning practices, including separating tuning seeds from testing seeds and using principled hyperparameter optimization over a broad search space. Separating these stages makes evaluation less dependent on the particular randomness that guided the settings search.

The study compares multiple leading optimization tools with hand-tuned configurations across reinforcement learning algorithms and environments. Automated approaches often achieve better performance with lower computational overhead. Based on these findings, the paper proposes community practices intended to improve reproducibility, strengthen empirical comparisons, and reduce computational costs. It also provides ready-to-use implementations of the tuning methods to make adopting these practices easier.
icml-2023-hyperparameters-in-reinforceme.tldr: Principled hyperparameter optimization and separate tuning and testing seeds can improve reinforcement learning evaluation, with automated tuning often outperforming hand-tuned configurations.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often propagate information using nonnegative operators shared across feature channels. These restrictions can limit the variety of transformations a network learns. Repeated propagation can also cause over-smoothing, making node features increasingly alike and restricting the usefulness of deeper networks.

The paper introduces omegaGNN, which learns channel-specific weights for mixing smoothing and sharpening operators at each layer. Smoothing combines nearby information, while sharpening supports maintaining distinctions. Allowing different channels to learn different mixtures gives graph propagation more flexibility, motivated by the diverse filters available to convolutional neural networks.

The authors study two versions, omegaGCN and omegaGAT. They theoretically analyze how the learned weights affect node features in omegaGCN, and experiments support the analysis and demonstrate how both variants avoid over-smoothing. Across 15 real-world datasets covering node and graph classification, the models perform comparably to leading methods. The contribution combines a readily implemented change to propagation with an explanation of how it affects the representations produced by deeper graph networks.
icml-2023-improving-graph-neural-network.tldr: OmegaGNN learns channel-specific mixtures of smoothing and sharpening operators, addressing over-smoothing while matching leading classification methods in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Explaining a prediction from multivariate time series requires identifying both the relevant features and the moments when they matter. A feature's influence can change with its position in time, so an explanation must account for temporal dependence as well as the presence of particular observations.

Perturbation-based saliency methods approach this by altering the input and learning a mask that identifies influential feature-time locations. Earlier methods learn the mask while keeping the perturbation rule fixed. The paper questions that choice because those fixed alterations were inspired by methods for static data, whose structure differs from temporal data.

The proposed approach learns the perturbations together with the masks. This lets the explanation procedure adapt both where it changes a time series and how it changes those locations. Empirical results show a significant improvement in explanation quality on time-series data. The finding makes the perturbation itself an important part of explanation design: the changes used to probe a prediction can affect how well the resulting saliency identifies relevant temporal information.
icml-2023-learning-perturbations-to-expl.tldr: Learning input perturbations alongside saliency masks significantly improves time-series explanation quality in the paper's experiments.

paragraphs: Online learning must keep updating as new data arrives, and the data distribution may change during training. This paper asks how stochastic gradient descent should adjust its learning rate in that setting. It designs schedules around regret, measuring performance through an objective that accounts for learning over time.

For online linear regression, an analysis using stochastic differential equations fully characterizes the optimal schedule. For general convex losses, the authors propose schedules robust to distribution shift and establish upper and lower regret bounds that agree up to constants. These results provide both achievable performance and a benchmark for judging how close it is to optimal.

For non-convex losses, the paper introduces a gradient-norm-based notion of regret and gives a schedule minimizing an upper bound on its total expectation. This is a different guarantee from the linear-regression characterization. The analysis confirms that optimal schedules typically use larger learning rates when distributions shift, consistent with needing greater adaptability. Experiments illustrate the proposed schedules and their regret behavior.
icml-2023-learning-rate-schedules-in-the.tldr: The paper derives learning-rate schedules for changing distributions, with guarantees tailored to linear regression, convex losses, and non-convex losses.

paragraphs: Understanding human motion involves reasoning about what happens, when it happens, and how different events relate. The paper introduces HumanMotionQA to evaluate these abilities on long motion sequences. Its question-answer dataset requires models to combine several reasoning steps rather than merely recognize an overall motion.

The questions involve finding motor cues in short portions of a sequence, reasoning about event timing, and retrieving particular motion attributes. This combination connects local evidence to longer temporal context. A model must therefore use detailed motion information while keeping track of relationships across the sequence.

The authors propose NSPose, a neuro-symbolic approach that combines learned motion representations with symbolic reasoning. Its modular design learns motion concepts, neural operators for attributes, and temporal relations that support answering questions. NSPose outperforms all baseline methods in the reported HumanMotionQA evaluation. The result supports this modular combination as a suitable approach to the task, while the dataset supplies a focused way to test complex reasoning about extended human motion.
icml-2023-motion-question-answering-via-.tldr: HumanMotionQA tests multi-step reasoning over long human motions, and the modular neuro-symbolic NSPose method outperforms its evaluated baselines.

paragraphs: Comparing numbers looks elementary, but learning reliable comparisons can be difficult for neural networks. The paper finds that both general-purpose multilayer perceptrons and the arithmetic-focused Neural Arithmetic Logic Unit struggle with this task. In the studied setting, neither extrapolates to numbers much larger than those encountered during training.

The authors introduce the Neural Status Register, a differentiable architecture designed to learn comparisons. Differentiability makes the comparison component compatible with neural learning. Its purpose is to provide a more suitable building block for tasks where decisions depend on numerical relationships.

Experiments validate the architecture in several settings and show how it can be combined with other neural models. Applications include piecewise-defined arithmetic, comparing digit images, recurrent problems, and finding shortest paths in graphs. The Neural Status Register outperforms all evaluated baseline architectures, with particularly strong results when extrapolating to larger numbers. These findings highlight comparison as a distinct capability that benefits from architectural support, especially when a model must operate beyond the numerical range of its training examples.
icml-2023-neural-status-registers-485605.tldr: Neural Status Registers improve learned numerical comparisons, especially extrapolation to larger numbers, and can be combined with other neural models.

paragraphs: Generating samples quickly from a pretrained diffusion model requires an efficient sampling procedure. Shortcut Fine-Tuning addresses this by optimizing the sampler directly using Integral Probability Metrics, which measure differences between distributions. The goal is to find an efficient route to good samples rather than make learning the reverse diffusion process the central objective.

This formulation allows a sampler to discover a shortcut that departs from the backward diffusion trajectory. Taking a control perspective, the authors develop SFT-PG, a policy-gradient version of Shortcut Fine-Tuning. They prove that, under certain assumptions, gradient descent on the diffusion model's distribution-matching objective is equivalent to a policy-gradient update.

Experiments show that the method can further improve existing fast DDPM samplers. Across the evaluated datasets, sample quality is comparable to or can exceed that of the full-step model. The work therefore links a practical fine-tuning strategy to reinforcement learning theory, while the equivalence remains conditional on the assumptions used in the proof.
icml-2023-optimizing-ddpm-sampling-with-.tldr: Shortcut Fine-Tuning directly optimizes fast diffusion samplers, using a conditional policy-gradient connection and achieving strong sample quality in experiments.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems aim to present relevant content, but optimizing accuracy can produce a narrow selection. Conventional diversification methods change which existing items are shown, for example through re-ranking. This paper considers an additional source of diversity: influencing the kinds of content that creators choose to produce.

The approach uses the performative nature of recommendation, meaning that the system's choices can change the content it will encounter later. Creators respond strategically to recommendation incentives. The proposed regularization anticipates those responses and penalizes content homogeneity, bringing expected changes in the supply of content into the learning objective.

The authors provide analytical and empirical results describing when and how these incentives can encourage diversity. Experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic data demonstrate the approach's utility. The contribution shifts attention toward the feedback between recommendations and content creation, offering a mechanism intended to support inherent, sustained diversity. Its evidence concerns the modeled strategic responses and the stated experimental settings, where anticipating creator behavior can help shape a more diverse content supply.
icml-2023-performative-recommendation-di.tldr: A recommendation regularizer anticipates creators' strategic responses to encourage the production of diverse content.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether two Gaussian databases are independent or correlated when the correspondence between their users is unknown. Each database has n users and d features. Under the correlated hypothesis, some unknown rearrangement of the rows aligns users whose data has correlation rho.

The authors study sharp thresholds separating statistically detectable and undetectable regimes. When d grows and rho squared times d tends to zero, even weak detection—doing slightly better than chance—is impossible, regardless of n. This result complements a simple test based on thresholding the sum of entries in the matrix product of the transposed first database with the second.

For fixed d as n grows, the paper establishes a dimension-dependent threshold below which strong detection, meaning error probability tending to zero, is impossible. Weak detection is also impossible when rho squared times d vanishes in this regime. These are limits on what any statistical test can accomplish under the model. Distinguishing weak from strong detection makes clear that some evidence of correlation and reliably vanishing error are different objectives.
icml-2023-phase-transitions-in-the-detec.tldr: The paper establishes statistical detection thresholds for correlated Gaussian databases whose user correspondences are hidden by an unknown permutation.

paragraphs: Rare outcomes can be difficult to predict because few examples are available. Many occur at the end of a sequence with more common intermediate outcomes, such as seeing an advertisement, clicking it, and purchasing. The paper shows theoretically and experimentally that earlier outcomes can help estimate the probability of the rare final event.

PRESTO relaxes the proportional-odds model used for ordered categories. Instead of sharing one set of feature weights across all category boundaries, it learns separate weights for each transition. An L1 penalty encourages corresponding weights in adjacent transitions to remain similar, allowing information sharing without requiring identical effects everywhere.

The authors prove consistent estimation of the boundary weights under a sparsity assumption. Synthetic and real-data experiments show better rare-probability estimation than logistic regression trained on the rare category and the more restrictive proportional-odds model. The results illustrate the benefit of balancing flexibility with shared structure: common stages contribute information, while each transition can retain its own relationship to the features.
icml-2023-predicting-rare-events-by-shri.tldr: PRESTO improves rare-event probability estimation by sharing information across ordered outcomes while allowing their feature effects to differ.

paragraphs: Learning against adversarial opponents in Markov games faces strong statistical and computational barriers. This paper studies a more structured situation: every agent follows the same learning procedure. That assumption leaves room for guarantees that adversarial-opponent impossibility results do not rule out.

The proposed algorithm achieves sublinear swap regret when all agents execute it, which also implies convergence to a correlated equilibrium. It is decentralized, computationally efficient, and requires no communication between agents. The guarantee therefore relies on a shared learning procedure while allowing agents to carry it out separately.

The key analysis connects policy optimization to weighted regret minimization. The relevant weights are unknown and depend on the path length of the agents' policy sequence, which captures how much their policies change over learning. Controlling that movement produces weighted objectives for which sufficiently adaptive algorithms achieve sublinear regret. This explains how coordinated choice of learning rule can support equilibrium convergence without communication, while preserving the essential condition that all participants use the proposed procedure.
icml-2023-regret-minimization-and-conver.tldr: When all agents use its procedure, a decentralized Markov-game algorithm achieves sublinear swap regret and convergence to a correlated equilibrium.

paragraphs: Spherical convolutional neural networks extend convolution to signals defined on a sphere. Computing these convolutions in the spectral domain offers accuracy and efficiency, but still costs more than ordinary planar convolution. This expense has restricted applications to smaller problems and models with limited capacity.

The paper tackles scaling through several connected changes. It introduces variants of familiar model components, implements core operations to take advantage of hardware accelerators, and designs input representations suited to particular applications and the model's properties. Together, these improvements allow larger spherical networks to address more demanding problems.

Experiments show leading performance on several prediction targets in the QM9 molecular benchmark, a setting previously dominated by equivariant graph neural networks. The larger models also achieve competitive results on multiple weather forecasting tasks. These findings demonstrate that spherical convolution can be useful beyond the small-scale settings imposed by its computational cost. The contribution combines model design, implementation, and input representation to make that increased scale effective in the reported applications.
icml-2023-scaling-spherical-cnns-2155338.tldr: Model, implementation, and representation improvements scale spherical CNNs to strong molecular prediction and competitive weather forecasting results.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient methods sometimes obtain samples by following a Markov chain, so successive samples depend on the sampling process's current state. This occurs in settings such as random-walker-based decentralized optimization, reinforcement learning, and online system identification. The paper studies convergence when the optimizer has access only to this kind of sampling.

The authors first establish a theoretical lower bound for methods that collect gradients along a Markov-chain path. The bound reveals a dependence on the chain's hitting time, connecting optimization difficulty to how the sampling process reaches states. They then analyze Markov-chain SGD under much milder regularity assumptions than earlier work.

The paper also introduces MC-SAG, a variance-reduced alternative to MC-SGD. Its dependence on the Markov chain is only through hitting time, leading to a communication-efficient token algorithm. Together, the lower bound and algorithmic results clarify how the sampling process constrains optimization and how variance reduction can address this setting. The work emphasizes obtaining guarantees while imposing fewer restrictions on both the chain and the optimized functions.
icml-2023-stochastic-gradient-descent-un.tldr: The paper links optimization under Markovian sampling to hitting time and introduces a variance-reduced method for communication-efficient decentralized learning.

paragraphs: Hypersphere classification can express classification decisions through geometric regions, offering explanations that are easy to process. Finding a concise explanation is substantially harder for binary data than for real-valued data. This paper investigates that difficulty through a complexity-theoretic study focused on binary inputs.

The analysis uses fine-grained parameterized complexity to separate the effects of different aspects of the problem. It considers structural properties in the data alongside restrictions on how concise the explanation must be. This perspective asks which features of an instance drive computational difficulty and which can support more efficient exact methods.

The results include stronger lower bounds and new fixed-parameter algorithms. The lower bounds sharpen the understanding of computational barriers, while the algorithms can find an exact, concise explanation when one exists. These contributions give a more differentiated account than treating all binary classification instances as equally difficult. They connect the demand for understandable explanations to the structure that makes finding those explanations algorithmically feasible under suitable parameterizations.
icml-2023-the-computational-complexity-o.tldr: The paper establishes computational barriers and fixed-parameter algorithms for finding exact, concise hypersphere explanations of binary data.
